Great preformance, no doubt. I own one myself. 

BUT ...... 

be careful. I have had a GTX 1070, and a GTX 1080 (right now) and both have trouble. The fans die (in the card), noises, lights not working anymore, and many other things. Now my games start to crash. I have had so much trouble with these 2 cards ... its unbelievable. My PC was brand new 1.5 years ago, everything is high end hardware and everything works fine, expect the card keeps giving me trouble. I saved 3 years for this amazing game PC, its such a sad thing that it keeps letting me down. 

Its a VERY GOOD gaming card performance wise, NO DOUBT, but I have had so much trouble with these 2 cards. The GTX 1070 literately broke after using it for not even 3 months. The shop got me a GTX 1080 as a 'sorry' but I had to pay the difference between the 2 cards, the GTX 1070 was 100% refunded (of course) so I chose to get the GTX 1080 and again experiencing weird problems. Lights not working, lots of noises, and now crashes of my games. Just a side note, I don't touch anything myself inside my PC. I let this all be done by professionals because I am very scared I screw something up myself. 

What is wrong with it ? I can;t believe its just a coincidence they both have trouble. come on, I payed like 800+ euro plus for it !! I DEMAND a card without trouble the coming years for that price.

I am just saying, watch out, there might be better options ? I don't know. The card itself, again, is amazing in performance. I play AC origins on ultra, I play Warhammer total war 2 on ultra, all no trouble at all performance wise, but many things are off with the card *in my case*. 


The temps are fine though. No trouble there.

Seiso Haou Sorry, not sure what you're saying other than frame time and I'm not sure what point you're making with it. It's just the inverted relationship from FPS, a different number saying the same thing.
It doesn't get cheaper, that's just how quickly the GPU is able to spit out a frame. If the GPU is very capable and produces a frame every 4ms, you'll get 240 FPS. If it is not capable and produces a frame every 32ms, you'll get 30 FPS. Resolution is one of the factors that determines how quickly a frame is produced, as higher resolutions are very taxing and bog the GPU down.

text:
Yes but FPS is not an accurate measure as it takes say 90 fps to get to 240 from 150 fps
90 fps is 11 ms
240 FPS is 4 ms and 150 fps is 6.6 ms
People tend just tend to think of it as each increase in FPS has the same value at all stages, but the higher you go, the less the value of each "frame" in FPS you're getting and the less power the GPU has to exert to get those extra "frames" at that high frame rate.  4K is a four-times increase over the standard resolution of games (1080p). In case you didn't notice, there is a colossal difference in computing power necessary to run something like that. The shift of focus to 4K for gaming happened too quickly for hardware to actually catch up. You truly are an utterly misguided human being if you think the Pascal series is a let-down; because, comparing the GTX 1xxx series to the GTX 9xx series, they have done an incredible amount of work to improve in such a short amount of time. text:
The "well-documented" problems with SLI seems to be a reach. SLI has worked well reliably for years for productive apps (a no-brainer) 

In 2016,  SLI is definitely a worthwhile investment   w/ VR (GPU per eye, AAA DirectX developers now more sure of the APIs from Microsoft what's available for multi-GPU arrangement; & the fact you still need to do SLI for optimal 1440p & 4K gaming—especially with ultra-wide monitors.

Sure, this past year and initial DirectX 12 games was not kind to SLI owners as dev shop sort out how to progressively enhance their games for DX12 & how much it was a honestly a hack pre DX12. Especially if some of them considered the Windows store limitations that didn't actually unlock multi-GPU set-ups (not until the summer apparently)

Vulkan doesn't have such issues, and VR APIs take this already into account, ensuring devs this with a support matrix that ensures  its utilization won't be hindered having to account for so much legacy GPUs. 

At the end of the day, it's not SLI problem, it was primarily the limitations of DX11 & etc. that's now being phased out aggressively by AMD, Nvidia, & Windows.

author: @MrJackZhan

text:
I'm going to go out on a limb because I haven't seen it personally in situations other than mine. Games+CAD Nvidia = Nice compromise. Both aspects perform well. (Ignore Quadro)

Pure CAD, AMD has it hands down with OpenCL and FirePro. It's so much faster with high polys.  I could be wrong as time has passed so as usual, never get complacent.
author: @miinyoo

text: +miinyoo Well I think you might have mixed up OpenCL and OpenGL. For CAD applications you will see OpenGL most of the time, which is used for graphics. OpenCL is for computation stuff only, and since CPUs and NVIDIA Tesla cards have dominated his area for a long time, you rarely see a AMD GPU in a pure computation setup. There are also way more software with CUDA support because most supercomputers with GPUs use NVIDIA GPUs.
author: @MrJackZhan

text:
On the last part, you're correct but Autodesk is taking advantage of OpenCL for acceleration of viewport which is tremendous when manipulating complex geometry at a productive speed.
Even rendering is moving in that direction. Not knocking CUDA because it is still "the king". Compared to OpenCL, however, it is only phantom king. CUDA is good and I wholly appreciate it in my day to day since I like the versatility to use it for both gaming and CAD (hence why I have a couple 980ti's). OCL is in practice much faster for the same silicon run on AMD FirePros. *at least for now as far as I have seen.
author: @miinyoo

text: +miinyoo NVIDIA used to have OpenCL support, but they have since discontinued development, probably in favor of their proprietary CUDA solutions. OpenCL is still included in current drivers, but it's only OpenCL 1.0 or 1.2, so you can't really do a lot with it. Thus we can't really compare CUDA and OpenCL right now since we can't run both (efficiently) on any hardware. As someone who write codes for these cards, I personally prefer CUDA because the kernel code for GPU is compiled with the CPU code, as opposed to OpenCL which compiles GPU code at runtime and requires a plaintext copy of the GPU code to go with the executable. I do appreciate OpenCL as a non-proprietary solution, though, and I hope NVIDIA will change their mind in the future and include OpenCL support.

text:
You know the reference cooler is NEVER better than what aftermarket can come up with. The blower may be better in certain cases and situations (like SLI), but most likely Nvidia's claim of "premium" components will at best amount to matching EVGA's, MSI's, Gigabyte's, or ASUS's mid-range coolers. 

Sure, the best aftermarket coolers like EVGA's Kingpin, MSI's Lightning, or Gigabyte's Windforce 3x will likely cost nearly what the reference (now called Founders Edition) costs, but they will [maybe] have binned chips with more overclock headroom meaning higher factory overclocks, and at the least the better coolers will allow overclocking without the card downclocking itself to stay under 90C.

My R9 390 (obviously puts off more heat than a 970 or 1080 and pretty close to a 980's thermals) has MSI's Twin Frozr V cooler on it and at max load with the fan at 80% it stays under 75C. I can bump the fan curve up to 100% to keep it under 70C and it's still barely audible (my cpu radiator fans are louder). The 1080 reference cooler has already been shown to hit 80C which is most likely 90% or 100% fan speed (I haven't seen anything to confirm or deny, based purely on 980 reference cooler) and is probably very audible.

TL;DR - Founders Edition may have better components than last gen, but it's still reference and fundamentally the same design. The cooler will remain the same while aftermarket coolers will continually improve (and get more expensive) and surpass the reference cooler.

To get a better idea of how Cross/SLI is for a specific game or games you are interested in, I would look up the Frame Time results of crossfiring whatever card you are interest in on that game. The FPS of crossfire/SLI don't really matter as much as the frame times. text:
People are getting upset with feeling underwhelmed by the 1080. People seemed to have expected double fps of last gen Nvidia cards, but they don't seem to understand the variables. Yea, the 1080 isn't as insanely powerful as they made it seem, but it's still got a 10-20% jump on last gen cards. 
First off, this card isn't even released yet, so optimization is going to be basically nowhere. So as drivers update, and games are optimized for the new hardware, expect another good 10-20% increase on top of what it is already. And not only that, this thing is (apparently) capable of overclocking to 2.1ghz like they showed at the stream. All the cards being used are running around 1500-1700mhz at stock clock and boost speeds. And I'm sure EVGA, Gigabyte and all them will eventually release cards that hit that beautiful 2ghz mark.
So stop complaining, and give it about 6 months. After proper optimizations are made, and partner companies start releasing over clocked editions, expect a MUCH larger gap beween Maxwell and Pascal. It won't just be "8-10 more fps", it'll probably be around 30-40 more by that point.
Regardless though, kind of relieved Pascal wasn't as overwhelmingly ground breaking as they made it sound on stream, because it means AMD doesn't have such a massive gap to fill in order to compete with Nvidia this year.
Nice review though :)

author: @olejnick9324

text:
+NinjaNickYT Well, it is supposed to give a theoretical boost in power, however in many cases it is heavily broken. On NVIDIA's side, it is called Scalable Link Interface, or SLI, from AMD's side, it is called Crossfire. SLI requires an additional component known as an SLI bridge, which acts as a bridge between connectors on the top of the cards, Crossfire does not require this. 

It is really only recommended for high end cards, a single higher end card is generally better than multiple lower end cards, and if there is no higher end card, then you go for multiple cards. The issue with it is that it is heavily broken simply because devs do not take the time to implement it as few people actually use it. New APIs for developers like DirectX12 and Vulkan now have their own versions of it that do not require things like SLI or crossfire, and can even be done between AMD and NVIDIA cards. 

Pros: 

More Power

Cons: 

More expensive, not really worth the money in most cases
Poorly implemented.

text:
Hey guys! Watching this video made me think about a very interesting benchmark metric that, I think, nobody ever published but would really help people plan which card they should go for when thinking about a long term solution. I was inspired by this idea after you mentioned the dollars per frame metric, which is a much more interesting metric than the score per dollar one that most people are using.

Basically, you said that the 1080, while being more interesting than a pair of 980 in SLI because of the price and the issues that comes with SLI, was still not powerful enough to properly beat the duo as per Nvidia's claims. While your numbers are perfectly agreeing with this, they do not take into account the 20 months of performance optimizations and bug fixes that have been put in the drivers and games since the release of the 980.

I would be very interested in seeing a comparison of benchmark scores over time as updates have been published. This would be an insanely tedious metric to gather, as you would need to run a set of benchmarks for each update that came out (or at least most of them) since the release of the original drivers. On the other side, it would give us a fair idea of how performance improves over the life of a GPU solely based on software changes which, in turns, can help people forecast how well their shiny new card should perform as it matures.

You said that the 1080 is still not enough to play games in 4k at a solid 60 frames per seconds. While this is true today, we have no way to know that this will be true in 3 or 4 months. Who knows if, as new game engines starts to abuse the new features of the card, things will get better. Even worst, besides numbers published in the drivers' release notes, we don't even know if the games actually perform better in the end as performance optimizations in one area of the code competes with bug fixes in an other.

text:
msh So there I got false informations or I don't find the correct video / article. 
It doesn't matter at all. 

So the ref. design or the founders edition (fe) will cost around 700$ BUT the board partner cards (like from Asus, EVGA and so) will start at 599$ which is (obviously) cheaper than a Fury X.

And my power consumption point:
The Fury X uses around 410w in a total system under normal load (http://www.anandtech.com/show/9390/the-amd-radeon-r9-fury-x-review/25).

This is (in euro):
0.41kWh x 5h x 0.24ct/kwh = 0.49€/day
0.41kWh x 5h x 30d x 0.24ct/kWh = 14.76€/month
0.41kWh x 5h x 360d x 0.24ct/kWh = 177.12€/year

Just with a Fury X, I might be wrong with this, but I don't think so. And still these aren't the same results all over the world, because the price per kWh changes from country to country. 

But now the new 1080:
We saw around 250W under load which leads me to the exception that this won't change much.
So my new results:

0.25kWh x 5h x 0.24ct/kWh = 0.3€/day
0.25kWh x 5h x 30d x 0.24ct/kWh = 9€/month
0.25kWh x 5h x 360d x 0.24ct/kWh = 108€/year


So with an average of 5h playing video games and letting this card run under load you're going to see the difference: 177€ per year vs 108€ per year. This is like 70€ difference. 

If you can buy a Fury X for like 625€ you'll be happy. But per year you'll pay around 177€ for using this card in your system which makes a total of 802€ after a year. 
The 1080 starts at 700€* in the f.e. and will cost around 108€ a year in your system. Is about 808. I admit: This card is more expensive but this is a brand new card. 

If you use a board partner card it looks totally different:
600€* + 108€ = 708€ ^^


so this was an hour of maths. I hope you enjoyed and understood what I wanted to tell you with that. And I only used like 10 Minutes on researching on the internet and about 5 Minutes to calculate every result :D

*: I used the conversion for 1:1 it's like 1$ = 0.92€, so it doesn't really matter ^^
Prices will increase or drop ^^ :D

+SomethingCool51 it's easy to see that you have little to no idea what you are talking about. 450watt 80+ bronze basicly means that it will be atleast 80% efficient at max usage. so if the TDP for the cpu is 120watt and the card is 250watt then a 450 80+ anthing would be more than enough if he doesn't have a high amount of other stuff in the pc such as multiple storage devices along with a lot of fans.


600 watt is overkill for most single card configs. 500-550watts is more than enough. and in some cases 450 could be enough with power to spare.

also the wattage of the PSU =/= the quality of the CPU. it's more down to internal components and thresholds and ratings. you need better quality components to get better efficiency for a PSU which is why PSU's with better ratings tend to be of better quality.

text:
+SomethingCool51 +Mortjep9531 The wattages they measured are from the entire system. Watch the video again.
It just doesn't make sense for this GPU to take 250 Watt of power.
1. They already made a huge jump in node shrink to 16mm FinFET when we have been stuck with 28nm for so long.
2. Even the 28nm Maxwell GPUs are so power efficient. So we would expect another considerable jump in power efficiency with the huge node shrink.
3. GTX 1080 uses only ONE 8-pin power connector.

text:
Lonewolf that first link I posted was less than two weeks after the launch of the Fury X. It has always outgunned the 980ti and Titan X at 4k. AMD just get better performance at higher resolutions. The same goes for my 390x's and the rival 980.

Nvidia are definitely better at the lower end, and at extreme refresh rates at 1080p. I'd even go so far as to suggest that the 750ti is the most remarkable card around, due to its staggering performance with no additional power connections. However, they just can't match AMD at 4k. text:
14supersonic The 1080 is a terrible price to performance option, and it always will be. Yes if you wait a year for Big Pascal to arrive you can get something better, but you can always make the argument for waiting outlandishly long times for something better instead of looking what's available now.

The second most powerful card in SLI is always always always the best cost/performance option. Right now that was the Fury or the 980 Ti, and by the time next month rolls around it will be the 1070.

We don't even know if P100 will even make it into a consumer chip. At the moment it looks wholly unsuited for gaming, it is first and foremost and extremely powerful compute device.

You keep talking about SLI but the fact is I have used SLI for five years now and not experienced the issues you are talking about. It's not even down to the devs to support SLI with Dx11, it is down to Nvidia to make the drivers for it. This changes for Directx 12 but only for API-based multi-adapter.

While we're on the subject of Dx 12, I do find it absolutely ludicrous that the first few games come out (I say "come out", most of the games are still in pre-alpha or Early Access) on a completely brand new API that is exclusive to an OS that is notoriously unstable and janky as all fuck when it comes to drivers, and these games don't support SLI that well and you're writing off SLI as a concept. Let the API develop, let Windows 10 mature, and then see where multi-GPU goes, before parroting off the same crap about SLI that hasn't been true for years.

The fact is that the "hassle" of SLI involves putting in a second card and enabling SLI in the driver, that stutter hasn't been a thing for years, and if you want to actually play at 4K ultra at 60 fps plus (up to 120Hz in the near future due to DP1.4) even on Pascal SLI is the only sodding way you're going to do it.

Its why Nvidia dropped support of more than 3 cards OFFICIALLY, you still could use it. At that point you get diminishing returns, and its not as efficient. Arguably the same thing can happen with 2 way if not done properly. So I'm not writing it off, like I said its good if you want to upgrade in the future, but if you are trying to beat a 1080 with two 1070's, then just get a 1080 now, and SLI later, or wait for a 1080Ti later this year, or early next year. Based on the trends Nvidia typically follows we know its coming so its not that hard. I'm not saying wait forever, I know how the GPU hardware cycle goes, and it can be a very money grabing thing on the companies part, and addicting on the users part. The key isn't gaming to see what is the next best thing that comes first. Its scoping out what you want, and then waiting to see if that new thing fits your needs, and I know in my case and many others that buying two cards out right isn't necessary at initial purchase.

As for the DX12 thing you mentioned you know there are more games than pre-alpha, or early access games that support DX12. Like you said there are a few, but Hitman, Rise of the Tomb Raider, Quantum Break, Gears of War Ultimate Edition, and Ashes of the Singularity (Which really isn't a game, its more of a benchmarking tool) all support DX12. You really think they care about putting it on Linux or Mac that get much less support overall than their platform. I don't blame them, and once they iron out the kinks in W10 no is going to really care at that point as long as their game perform like they should.

The point is that the performance difference is tiny and the price difference is huge, so for cost to performance it always makes more sense to get two of the second tier, than one of the top when they are both based on the same GPU.

Both Nvidia and AMD do this like clockwork for the last few generations. They did it with the 780, 970, 980 Ti, 290, 390, Fury... the exceptions would be the older cards when the second tier was a rebranded former top tier and not a cut down version of the same GPU at all, such as the GTX 770.

text: Normally I don't comment, but I've got to point out that we don't know how these two cards were compared. Given that this was recorded in Mexico, I'm wondering if these FPS numbers were from the Nvidia showing and Titan X numbers were pulled from prior experience? If so then this isn't a direct apples to apples comparison. For example, we don't know what processors the Nvidia rig might have been using, nor it's RAM or any of the other components. In addition, when you look at the posted specs of both of these cards, the Titan X has 512 more cuda cores and could easily be pushed to the same speeds as a stock 1080. The Titan X is 3Gb/s slower for it's memory clock, but has a slightly higher overall Bandwidth (336.5 vs 320). So, lets get as close to an apples to apples comparison on these two and see exactly how much more of an improvement the 1080 is before bowing down to the new GPU god.
